KEY MESSAGE 1...
After a mild morning with lows in the upper 40s and 
mid 50s today, unusually warm weather for late fall is expected this 
afternoon. With the high pressure system having moved to our east 
off the Atlantic coast, the upper level ridge currently positioned 
over western. NY will begin to slide east with the ridge axis 
centered overhead our region by mid morning/early afternoon. 
Southerly flow continues to help advect a moist airmass into the 
region with PWAT's gradually rising to near 1" along with dewpoints 
increasing into the 50s by afternoon. However with broad subsidence 
occurring over the region, any lingering low stratus in the morning 
should clear up with daybreak allowing for a mostly clear day across 
the region. Current model guidance show 850 mb ensemble anomalies 
increasing to +2 to +3 STDEV above normal and 850 mb temperatures 
ranging from about 12 to 15 degrees C, which is unusually warm for 
this time of year. High temperatures are expected to reach into the 
lower to mid 70s in the valley regions and into the upper 60s in the 
higher terrain areas today, potentially becoming close to just a few 
degrees shy of today's daily high records (the best chance at KGFL 
and KPOU with daily high records of 73 and 74F respectively). 
Probabilistic guidance has a high chance (70 to 90%) for much of the 
region to reach or exceed 70F and a medium to high chance (50 to 
80%) for reaching or exceeding 75F in parts of the Mohawk and 
Schoharie valley. Normal daily highs for this time of year across the 
region are typically in the low to mid 50s. Breezier conditions are 
also expected with gusts up to 10-15 kts in the afternoon and 
evening, particularly in the N/S oriented valleys and southerly 
facing slopes.

KEY MESSAGE 2... 
Thursday morning, a low pressure system tracks from 
the Great Lakes region into southeast Quebec as its associated cold 
front approaches from the west. Out ahead of the the cold front, a 
band of showers enters the region, initially in the west/southwest 
ADKs and western Mohawk Valley just before sunrise Thursday morning. 
Long range deterministic and ensemble guidance then show the showers 
overspreading the Capital Region and the rest of eastern NY by late 
morning before lessening in coverage into the afternoon/evening as 
it arrives into western New England. PWAT's rise above the 75th 
climatological normal to 1 to 1.5" Thursday, along with the NAEFS 
ensemble anomalies increasing to +3 to +4 STDEV, however the better 
upper level forcing still looks to be to the west of the Hudson 
River Valley. Expected highest rainfall amounts Thursday to be in 
the southwestern ADKs with the latest probabilistic NBM guidance 
showing a 50 to 60% chance of 0.75" or greater in this area, while 
areas along and south and east of I-90 generally receiving less than 
0.50" (only 40 to 50% probability of 0.25" or greater). Most 
locations will receive about a tenth of an inch of rain, which will 
be the most widespread measurable rainfall in close to 20 days for 
the region and therefore expected to bring an end to the recent dry 
spell. Thursday's highs will still run above normal in the  mid 60s 
to around 70F in the valleys and in the upper 50s to low/mid 60s in 
the higher terrain. There will also be more noticeable humidity 
compared to lately with dewpoints increasing into the 60s. Breezy 
conditions will continue with gusts 15-20 kts.

The low pressure system over the Great Lakes region closes off to 
our west Friday night. As the positively tilted trough begins to 
enter western NY Friday night into Saturday morning, additional rain 
showers are expected along it's frontal boundary. Latest model 
guidance has the closed low tracking overhead Saturday, however 
there is still some variability of the timing and track of this wave 
of low pressure and front. The latest medium and long range models 
have a heavier axis of rain showers in areas south and east of the 
Capital Region Friday and Friday night with rainfall totals up to 1" 
in these ares and lighter amounts in the Capital Region and areas 
north and west. 24-hr NBM probabilistic guidance has a 30 to 40% 
chance for 1" or greater and a 60 to 70% chance for 0.50" or greater 
in parts of Dutchess, Litchfield, and Berkshire counties. There is a 
40% or less chance for 0.50" or greater elsewhere. Much of the 
greater totals look to be south and east of our region at this time. 
Due to the recent dry spell, the rain will be beneficial and hydro 
issues are not anticipated at this time. Lingering isolated showers 
are possible into Saturday. Temps trend near to slightly below 
normal for the close of the weekend. The cooler and unsettled 
weather looks to continue into early next week.
